idiom_name: ordered handler interface + successor link + explicit terminal handler
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one request-handling operation and compose handlers through a successor link, ordered list, or injected next callable. Decide up front whether this is pure first-handler-wins, a multi-stage middleware pipeline, or an interceptor-style before/after chain; make each link's handle/forward contract explicit, assemble order from validated configuration, and terminate with an observable default result. Keep requests explicit and immutable where possible, and keep handler instances free of per-request state.
code_sketch:
interface Handler { Result handle(Request r); }          # + successor(next)
chain = build(configured_steps)                          # order fixed by policy
for h in chain:
    result = h.handle(request)
    if result is HANDLED: return result                  # first taker stops
return unhandled(request)                                # explicit terminal case
pitfalls: Omitting the terminal handler and letting unclaimed requests vanish silently.
Handlers that both do work and unconditionally forward, which turns the chain into a decorator stack and breaks the stop/pass contract.
Rewiring the chain at runtime without making the mutation thread-safe.
Async handler that does not await next() before returning, causing the chain to stall or produce an incomplete result before downstream handlers have run.
Mutable shared state on the handler instance (e.g. a counter, cache, or flag) that bleeds between concurrent requests when the same handler instance serves multiple clients simultaneously.
A circular successor reference between handlers creating an infinite forwarding loop; detect at startup by walking the chain and marking visited nodes.
Skipping the terminal handler to save a handler slot, so requests that reach the end of the chain are silently discarded with no logging or fallback response.
Handlers that consume the request body or cursor before forwarding, making retries or replay impossible for downstream handlers.
Absence of timeout middleware: a slow or hung handler in the middle of the chain blocks the entire request; always wrap the chain or individual handlers with deadline-gated execution.
Value-type handlers (e.g. structs) causing copy-related issues and unintended state loss as the request passes by value through each link.
Async-in-sync chains: mixing async and sync handler signatures in the same chain without a unified wrapper, causing unhandled promises, deadlocks, or silent stalls in production.
A branch that neither returns a result nor invokes its successor leaves request-oriented chains waiting forever; make every branch explicitly handle, forward, or fail with a bounded error.
Registering authentication or validation after a route or terminal handler lets protected work run before the guard; encode ordering constraints in the builder and test the composed chain.

Calling next() or chain.doFilter() twice - for example from a retry callback and its normal path - runs downstream work twice and can duplicate writes; make forwarding single-shot and return after short-circuiting.

Wrong move: sharing one handler instance across pipelines or threads while it keeps per-request state in fields -> concurrent requests read each other's data -> instead keep handlers stateless or mark them shareable only after proving thread-safety (Netty's @Sharable contract).

Wrong move: treating every middleware chain as first-handler-wins -> stages that must run on the response path (compression, headers, telemetry) never execute -> instead decide per chain whether links wrap the successor and run unwinding work, or consume-and-stop, and encode that in the handler contract.

Wrong move: piling cheap handlers onto a hot-path chain because each one is individually small -> dispatch overhead and opaque stack traces compound and latency regressions become unattributable -> instead keep closed-set decisions as a switch or lookup and instrument per-handler latency before adding links.
